# Outlook {#sec-outlook}

Starting prompt for this chapter: Chapter 11 concludes the book with a forward-looking assessment of AI in microscopy, focusing on how it can/will enable biological discovery. It should highlight a few motivational examples of discoveries that AI has already enabled and discuss opportunities to which the reader is primed to contribute after reading this book.

With this book, we hope to have set you on a journey of exploration into the use of AI methods in microscopy. In the final chapter, we reflect on some of the field's early successes and share our excitement for its future directions. Finally, we’ll look ahead to the path before you — how you can build on what you've learned to not only answer specific biological questions, but contribute to the broader advancement of this rapidly evolving domain.

## Early birds: breakthrough AI applications across biological domains
### Connectomics
The field of connectomics aims to reconstruct and analyze complete neural circuit diagrams. Microscopy for connectomics faces the combined challenge of requiring a very high resolution for individual synapse detection and a very large field of view for complete neuron tracing. Up until the very recent advances in Expansion Microscopy, Electron Microscopy remained the only modality suitable for connectomics studies, routinely generating tens to hundreds to thousands of Terabytes of image data at nanoscale resolution.  As the infeasibility of fully manual analysis became obvious with the first significant volume acquisitions (the first c elegans connectome from [White et al, 1988] required 10 years of manual tracing!), neuroscientists sought collaboration with machine learning and computer vision experts to speed up and automate neuron segmentation and synapse detection. Already the first such algorithms (refs) started to alleviate the manual annotation burden, while the rapid progress of the computer vision field in the new age of deep learning has allowed for more and more automated pipelines, complete with AI-based circuit error detection and correction. Beyond direct scaling of the circuit tracing process, new approaches have been proposed to complete tasks which were previously deemed infeasible, such as neurotransmitter prediction directly from EM images of synapses. The future of connectomics, expanding into larger and larger volumes up to the whole mouse brain or substantial pieces of the human brain (cite smth from Lichtmann), is tightly coupled to the progress in AI-based analysis which keeps reshaping our understanding of what is possible (cite google last paper).  

### In situ cryo-Electron Tomography
Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) images biological samples preserved as vitreous ice with transmission electron microscopy, tilting the sample in serial imaging to achieve volumetric acquisition. Combined with computational post-processing, this technique yields the highest resolution in all of biological imaging, allowing for Ångstrom-level investigation of macromolecular complexes. Here, image analysis challenges come from both technical and biological limitations. On the technical side, the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio (electron dose has to be limited to avoid damaging the sample) and the missing wedge artifact (the imaging is tomographic and not all angles can be achieved) make reliable segmentation and particle identification difficult even for human vision. On the biological side, the frontier application of cryo-ET to intact bacteria or cellular lamellae captures a very crowded and heterogeneous environment, further complicating image interpretation. AI has already integrated deeply into cryo-ET workflows, automating and accelerating many previously manual or challenging steps. With AI enabling faster and smarter data collection, the vision of near-unattended workflows is becoming increasingly attainable. 

### Imaging development
Development transforms a single cell into a complex organism through coordinated cell divisions, movements, shape changes and differentiation. Modern light-sheet microscopes can capture these processes across entire living embryos with high spatial and temporal resolution, producing volumetric time-lapse recordings in which tens of thousands of cells must be segmented and tracked over hundreds or thousands of frames. Both tasks are challenging at this scale: cells divide, deform and become densely packed, while tracking algorithms must preserve identities, detect divisions and remain robust to segmentation errors that can propagate through complete lineage trees. Continued progress in AI-based segmentation is improving developmental analysis pipelines, while the first methods to treat tracking itself as a deep learning problem are now beginning to emerge (cite Trackastra). Together, these advances bring us closer to turning whole-embryo movies into quantitative records of every cell’s behaviour and history (cite Loïc’s zebrafish and Katie’s mouse work), ultimately enabling systematic comparisons across embryos, perturbations and species.

### Multimodal integration in large-scale experiments
High-throughput microscopy experiments are reaching an extraordinary scale, producing hundreds of terabytes of data and images of billions of cells across tens or hundreds of thousands of chemical and genetic perturbations (cite JUMP). At the same time, new experimental platforms are beginning to measure several complementary aspects of cellular state, pairing morphological imaging with readouts such as gene expression, protein abundance and spatial organisation(cite Way; CRISPRmap; Perturb-Multimodal). Integrating these modalities is challenging as they differ in dimensionality, resolution, and experimental biases, while each captures only a partial view of the biological response. Early AI-based studies have shown that imaging, transcriptomic and chemical representations can be combined to improve the identification of related perturbations and mechanisms-of-action (cite Moshkov), while newer cross-modal and generative models are beginning to succeed in cross-modality prediction. The longer-term ambition of these efforts is the development of Virtual Cells: computational models that integrate diverse measurements of cellular state and predict how cells will respond to previously unseen perturbations (cite Arc Virtual Cell; CZI/Biohub Virtual Cells). Although such models remain at an early stage, they point towards a future in which large parts of cellular experimentation can first be explored in silico, guiding which hypotheses and interventions should be tested in the laboratory.

### Image restoration and virtual staining
As discussed in Chapter 6, AI-based image restoration is becoming an increasingly important part of modern microscopy. Restoration models can suppress noise, compensate for optical degradation, improve spatial or temporal resolution, and reconstruct useful images from measurements acquired with fewer photons or less sampling. This can enable faster, deeper and gentler imaging, extending the duration of live-cell experiments and revealing structures or dynamics that would otherwise be difficult to observe. Related virtual-labelling approaches can predict fluorescence-like representations from label-free or sparsely labelled images. However, because these models generate image content rather than simply measure it, their outputs may contain plausible-looking errors unsupported by the acquired data, making trustworthiness a central challenge. Many restoration problems are also intrinsically ill-posed, with several images potentially consistent with the same measurement. Emerging approaches therefore aim to represent distributions of plausible outputs and provide spatially resolved, calibrated uncertainty estimates that indicate where a reconstruction or virtual label may be unreliable (cite Jug lab/MicroSplit). Together, these developments are shifting AI towards an integral—and increasingly uncertainty-aware—part of the imaging process itself.

## Why it's a good time to start with DL for microscopy now?
- There is a lot of know-how accumulated in the field, existing architectures work well, new ones promise even more
- coding itself is getting much easier with new AI tools, see chapter 10. 
- Specific resources are starting to appear, including this book
- Existing DL tools are quite powerful, but require understanding of limitations. While it's tempting to just use things and move on to the next analysis step, you can get much more out of them if you have an idea about the internals.
- It provides a strategic advantage for the analysis of challenging data: large, volumetric, high-throughput, temporal. Screening, sorting, finding an elusive phenotype, for these and other applications the performance of your DL will define what is possible.



## What's next?
- DL is developing in a fast and very inpredictable way. No one asked in 2015 would have come forward with what we have now. 
- Over the last years, we have seen that foundation models trained on natural image data are finally starting to become useful for microscopy (see all recent DinoV2 examples). Considering humans train themselves to perform microscopy-related vision tasks by finetuning/repurposing their natural vision abilities, we might come to the point where the same will be true for DL models - we will use natural image ones directly, re-train self-supervised on large amounts of target domain data or supervised on a very particular dataset. 
- For image restoration, uncertainty estimation will only become more critical. New downstream algorithms will have to be developed that can take this uncertainty into account. 
- DL will move into analysis. See the first work on identifying phenotypes (our MorphoFeatures), finding sub-cellular protein distribution patterns (SubCell), analyzing mechanical forces (great paper, will find reference), etc. 

## How to continue from here? 
- Open source and open science: check how others train networks in their public models on the BioImage Model Zoo or Hugging Face. Contribute your models, with full metadata and training/validation notebooks. 
- - Come back to the critical importance of data. Architectures and networks come and go, data remains the foundation of what we do. Short overview of how to make your AI-ready data FAIR.

## Code and Equations {#sec-equation}

This is an example of including a python snippet that generates a figure

```{python}
#| label: fig-simple
#| fig-cap: "Simple Plot"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1,23,2,4])
plt.show()
```


In some cases, you may want to include a code-block that is not executed when the book is compiled. Use the `eval: false` option for this.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1,23,2,4])
plt.show()
```


Figures can also be generated that do not show the code by using the option for `code-fold: true`.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-polar
#| fig-cap: "A spiral on a polar axis"
#| fig-alt: "A line plot on a polar axis. The line spirals out from a value of zero to a value of 2."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

r = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01)
theta = 2 * np.pi * r
fig, ax = plt.subplots(
  subplot_kw = {'projection': 'polar'} 
)
ax.plot(theta, r)
ax.set_rticks([0.5, 1, 1.5, 2])
ax.grid(True)
plt.show()
```
